messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Liam, a 21-year-old man, found his world irrevocably altered six months ago. He and his wife, Sarah, were walking home one evening when they were suddenly accosted. Two figures emerged from an alley, moving with an unsettling, predatory slowness that Liam now recognises as the start of what felt like an inevitable disaster. One of them, a man with a distinctive tattoo on his forearm, lunged for Sarah’s bag. In the ensuing struggle, Sarah was violently pushed, her head hitting the pavement with a sickening thud. Liam remembers the metallic tang of blood mixing with the cheap, cloying scent of the attacker’s cologne as they fled. He saw the specific, intricate details of the tattoo on the man’s arm as he vanished into the darkness, an image seared into his mind. Bystanders quickly gathered, their hushed comments about Sarah’s condition feeling like an assault in themselves, focusing on his injured wife, his family.

In the aftermath, Liam found himself trapped in a relentless loop of memory. Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in his mind, vivid, static images of Sarah on the ground, the tattoo, the fleeing figures. Sometimes, when he thinks about that night, he can still smell that cheap cologne, or the faint, coppery scent of blood. He often struggles to articulate the full horror of it; he can't seem to put the frightening event into words, experiencing it more as a visceral, nonverbal assault on his senses.

Now, six months on, Liam lives in a state of constant alert. He finds himself immediately on guard if he notices people acting suspiciously, or if someone makes a sudden movement near him, his body tensing, his heart racing. He’s often plagued by flashbacks, moments where he is suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, the smells, the sights, the terror flooding his awareness. These intrusive experiences, coupled with a pervasive sense of unease, make it incredibly difficult for him to relax. He struggles with trouble falling or staying asleep, his mind replaying the event or scanning for potential threats even in the quiet of the night.

To cope, Liam has built walls around himself. Being unemployed means he spends a lot of time at home, but he finds it unbearable to be alone in a room or building; the quiet allows the memories to rush in, making him feel vulnerable. He often follows Sarah from room to room or insists on having the television on, even if he’s not watching it. He also actively avoids media, refusing to watch TV programmes or films, or read about similar events, terrified of encountering anything that might echo that terrible night. When the overwhelming feelings do break through his defences, the panic and distress becoming unbearable, he has, on occasion, hurt himself physically to release those feelings, a desperate attempt to regain some control over his internal chaos.

Liam has come to believe that his body keeps reacting as if he is still in danger even when he is safe, a frustrating betrayal that leaves him feeling exhausted and constantly on edge. He feels profoundly altered by the experience, convinced that he is no longer capable of doing the things that defined him before, a sentiment that weighs heavily on him given his current unemployment. He used to be an avid runner, a keen amateur photographer, but now he feels a deep sense of incapacity, unable to engage in activities he once loved. More fundamentally, he has lost faith in his own ability to navigate the world, certain that he can't rely on himself to protect those he loves or even to manage his own reactions. The cumulative toll of these changes has become too much to bear. Sarah, worried by his increasing withdrawal and the physical marks he sometimes bears, urged him to seek help. Liam comes to therapy hoping to find a way to quiet the relentless internal alarm, to feel safe in his own skin again, and to understand how he might ever reclaim the person he once was.
